To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the form of the microbial richness‐climate relationship varies among microbial groups and that this variation is explained by differences in resource ecology and limiting conditions for the different groups.

microbial communities along a tropical elevation–climate gradient are structured by environmental factors, but the nature of these responses is heterogeneous among taxa, and the richness–climate relationship for any given taxonomic group is often unimodal or linear.

the richness‐climate relationships for Fungi, Archaea, and Bacteria were all significantly different from each other along an elevation‐climate gradient, with fungal richness being strongly positively correlated with elevation, archaeal richness being negatively correlated with elevation, and bacterial richness showing a unimodal relationship with elevation, with the peak richness occurring at an elevation of approximately 1000 meters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the factors that determine species richness in microbial communities.
the relationship between microbial diversity and climate, and how this relationship is influenced by resource availability and other environmental factors.
understanding the drivers of biodiversity and community assembly in soil microbial communities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
microbial communities are not structured by climate, but rather by the environmental conditions that climate drives.

the community composition of soil microbes is strongly related to climate and resource availability along an elevation gradient in Hawaii, and that the form of these responses is related to the ecologies of the microbial groups.
the microbial communities are responding to climate change in a complex manner, with the response depending on the microbial group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the richness‐climate relationships for Fungi, Bacteira and Archaea along this gradient are all positive, with the form of these relationships being driven by resource availability and limiting conditions for the different groups.
there is no general pattern of richness along a tropical elevation–climate gradient, with the exception that the most abundant and diverse taxa occur in a narrow range of climate conditions.
microbial communities along a climate gradient are complex and variable, but that their responses are predictable and can be understood in the context of their resource‐ecology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are strong and predictable responses in microbial community structure to environmental gradients and that these responses are driven by the ecologies of the individual taxa.
microbial communities respond to environmental change at the same scales as plants and animals, and that microbial responses can differ in form from those of macroscopic organisms.
there are no general rules for how microbial communities respond to climate change.
